newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba reinforces coast patrols to monitor exiles.
newsitem.headline: Cuba reinforces coast patrols to monitor exiles.

text.p: Cuba reinforced patrols of its waters on Monday as Miami-based exiles flew near the island to mark the first anniversary of the downing by Cuban MiG fighters of two small planes flown by exiles.
There were no incidents. In Miami the U.S. Coast Guard said a fleet of Cuban exile planes was making its way safely back to Miami after dropping wreaths in the Florida Strait.
The planes flew to a point about 22 miles (35 kms) off Cuba's northern coast, where the United States says the planes were downed in international waters on Feb. 24 1996.
Cuba says the Cessna flown by an exile group called Brothers to the Rescue were shot down within Cuba's 12-mile territorial limit. The four fliers were killed in the incident.
Several dozen local and foreign reporters, invited by Cuban authorities, travelled out to sea on a naval submarine chaser on what officials called an observation mission.

The submarine chaser sailed to around 10 miles (16 kms) north of Havana. From there, a U.S. Coast Guard vessel could be seen on the horizon, marking the spot where the exile planes flew to drop their wreaths.
The Cuban Foreign Ministry, warning exile groups it would not tolerate territorial violations, had said last week Cuba would use any means necessary to prevent such violations.
The plane downings last year sparked international outrage and prompted the United States to toughen its longstanding economic embargo on Cuba.
President Fidel Castro's government said it acted in legitimate self-defence. It said the planes were violating Cuban airspace and had ignored warnings to leave.
Washington said the incident was an act of brutality. It said the planes were over international waters and wherever they were, they should not have been brought down with force.

The names of the four exiles killed in the incident were read out and remembered during a mass on Monday morning at one Havana church. The names, part of a customary list of people to be mourned, were apparently included by relatives.

Cuban authorities reiterated on Monday that the plane downings could have been prevented by the United States. An article in the weekly newspaper Trabajadores said Washington should have acted to prevent territorial violations by Cuban exile groups.

The newspaper noted that Cuba had clearly warned in January 1996 that it might use force to prevent territorial violations. It added U.S. authorities had been fully aware of the situation and of the exile group's plans, but had not acted.

The public warning by Cuba that it might use force was issued on Jan. 15, 1996, following incidents one week before when anti-government leaflets were scattered on Havana and surrounding areas by Brothers to the Rescue planes.

Havana said at the time its patience was running out after numerous violations of its territory over the previous 20 months. Brothers to the Rescue president Jose Basulto said the leaflets were scattered from outside Cuba's 12-mile territorial limit and winds carried them over Cuba.
